title: The phantom pilot said to haunt Liverpool's old airport
excerpt: The shadowy figure of a man has been spotted on numerous occasions
content:
A pioneering pilot who made aviation history is said to have never truly left Liverpool, with a ghostly figure reportedly spotted pacing around the hangar where he met his tragic end. Captain Thomas Campbell Black was once one of Britain's most celebrated aviators, winning an extraordinary air race in the 1930s before his life was cut short in a horrific accident at Speke Airport, now Liverpool John Lennon Airport.

But according to local ghost stories, his connection to the former airport did not end with his death.

As recounted by author John Reppion in his book 800 Years of Haunted Liverpool, the shadowy figure of a man has been spotted on numerous occasions around what was once Hangar Number One, where Black's aircraft was kept.

Some believe the apparition is the captain himself, still searching for another plane or trapped in a ghostly repetition of the events leading up to his death.

‌

And one particularly strange incident, involving an old airport lift and two night-shift workers, has helped keep the story alive.

The pilot who made aviation history

Speke Airport, which later became RAF Speke, was once one of the UK's oldest operational airports.

Scheduled flights began leaving the site in 1930, before the airport was officially opened on July 1, 1933.

It was here that Captain Thomas Campbell Black became a household name after teaming up with co-pilot Charles William Anderson Scott to win the London to Melbourne Centenary Air Race in 1934.

‌

Also known as the MacRobertson Air Race, the pair completed the journey in a record-breaking 71 hours.

Their victory earned them the Britannia Trophy and a huge £10,000 prize, making them international aviation celebrities. But just two years later, Black's promising career came to a tragic end.

A fatal collision at Speke

In September 1936, Black was preparing to compete in another major aviation challenge, the Schlesinger Race from England to Johannesburg, which offered another £10,000 prize.

‌

He was among the favourites to win and was preparing his Percival Mew Gull aircraft, newly christened Miss Liverpool, for take-off.

But on September 19, disaster struck. A Hawker Hart bomber, piloted by Officer Peter Stanley Salter, came in to land and collided with Black's aircraft.

The bomber's propeller tore through the side of the cockpit and struck the captain. Despite efforts to save him, Black died on the way to hospital.

The ghost in Hangar Number One

In the years that followed, stories began circulating of a mysterious male figure seen pacing around what was once Hangar Number One, where Miss Liverpool had been kept.

‌

Some believed it was Black's ghost, perhaps still searching for an aircraft or forever reliving the moments before his fatal collision.

According to Reppion, reports of the phantom continued among airport employees right up until the old site's closure in the mid-1980s.

One account, recorded in Jack Currie's book Echoes in the Air, recounts a particularly unsettling experience involving two employees working overnight in the airport's control tower in the 1970s.

'Bloody Captain Black again'

Mike Rudkin, a former Speke Airport employee, recalled working alongside colleague Dave Wilkinson during a quiet night shift.

‌

Rudkin had heard stories about the ghostly captain from workmates but admitted he had never put much faith in them.

However, he said there was always something forbidding about the old airfield, particularly after dark.

One evening, the pair were sitting in the control tower when their quiet night was interrupted by a tremendous crash coming from the building's ancient lift.

The elevator had apparently been summoned to the ground floor, but there was a problem.

‌

The lift dated back to the 1930s and had a heavy iron gate which had to be opened and closed by hand. Moving it made a distinctive noise which could easily be heard from the top of the tower.

But despite hearing the lift arrive, neither man heard the familiar clank of the gate. When Rudkin tried to summon the lift back upstairs, nothing happened.

He eventually forced open the shaft doors and peered down into the darkness, only to discover the elevator was nowhere to be seen.

With no explanation for what had happened, the men contacted the fire service for help.

‌

When firefighters arrived, they could find no sign of the lift on the ground floor. They eventually discovered it had travelled into the basement, which was still heavily padlocked.

After forcing their way inside, they found the cold, damp basement completely empty. But the lift's heavy iron gate was wide open.

According to Rudkin, when the firemen explained what had happened, his colleague Dave Wilkinson simply looked at him wearily and said: “Bloody Captain Black again".

A phantom still in the skies?

The old Speke Airport site has since been transformed, with the original buildings becoming part of a business park including Crowne Plaza Liverpool John Lennon Airport Hotel.

‌

The modern Liverpool John Lennon Airport is located around two miles south-west of the original airport site. But stories of strange happenings have continued to surround the area.

There have also been reports over the years of so-called phantom planes appearing above Speke and neighbouring districts.

While some sightings may simply have been light aircraft, others have suggested that Captain Thomas Campbell Black somehow took to the skies once more.
